lesson.title: Martin Luther King Jr. and the Making of a Movement Leader
lesson.summary: A young Baptist minister thrust into leadership almost by circumstance during the Montgomery Bus Boycott, Martin Luther King Jr. built on his theological training and study of nonviolent resistance to become the era's most influential civil rights leader.
lesson.body:
Martin Luther King Jr. was born on January 15, 1929, in Atlanta, Georgia, the son of Martin Luther King Sr., pastor of the influential Ebenezer Baptist Church. He grew up steeped in the Black church tradition and in a family that valued education, attending Morehouse College before pursuing seminary training at Crozer Theological Seminary in Pennsylvania and then a doctorate in systematic theology at Boston University, which he completed in 1955. That academic training exposed him deeply to the Social Gospel tradition, which held that Christian faith demanded action against social injustice, and to the writings of Mohandas Gandhi, whose philosophy of organized, disciplined nonviolent resistance against British colonial rule in India offered King a practical model, not just a moral one, for challenging segregation.

In 1954, King accepted a position as pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery, Alabama, a modest first pastorate for a man still in his mid twenties. He had barely settled into the role when the Montgomery Bus Boycott began in December 1955. Local organizers elected King to lead the newly formed Montgomery Improvement Association in part precisely because he was new to the city and had not yet made enemies or been drawn into local factional disputes, a choice that placed one of the century's most consequential leaders at the head of a movement almost by circumstance as much as by design.

Leading the boycott for 381 days tested and sharpened King's approach. He insisted on strict nonviolent discipline even as boycotters faced arrests, threats, and the bombing of his own home, and he proved skilled at explaining the movement's goals in language that could move both Black congregations and, increasingly, a national audience following the story in newspapers and on television. The boycott's success, combined with his standing as a minister, made King a natural choice to help lead a new organization in 1957, the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, which extended the Montgomery model of church based nonviolent protest to other Southern cities.

In the years that followed, King became the most visible national figure associated with the civil rights movement, a role that brought him into direct, and at times uneasy, contact with a rising generation of younger, more impatient activists who organized under groups like the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. King's insistence on nonviolence as both a moral principle and a practical strategy, one meant to win over public opinion by making the brutality of segregation visible, would be tested severely in the campaigns still to come, including the confrontation the movement mounted in Birmingham, Alabama, in 1963.
